item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"In SCOPe 2.08, NAD(P)-related enzymes/domains are not one homologous group. They appear in several separate folds and superfamilies, for example c.2.1 NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains (SUNID 51735, fold c.2), c.3.1 FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain (SUNID 51905, fold c.3), c.25.1 ferredoxin reductase-like C-terminal NADP-linked domain (SUNID 52343, fold c.25), d.58.20 NAD-binding domain of HMG-CoA reductase (SUNID 55035, fold d.58), and e.52.1 NAD kinase/diacylglycerol kinase-like (SUNID 111331, fold e.52). This implies convergence at the level of cofactor binding and redox/adenosine-phosphate chemistry: different ancestral scaffolds independently evolved pockets that bind NAD, NADP, FAD/NAD(P), or related ligands. Within a SCOPe superfamily, homology is implied; within a family it is stronger and usually supports closer functional transfer. But SCOPe fold and class placement alone do not imply homology, and the API homology endpoints explicitly warn that levels above superfamily do not imply homology. Therefore, similarity in bound cofactor, glycine-rich/adenosine-binding motifs, catalytic residues, or active-site geometry is insufficient by itself to infer common ancestry, transfer a full enzymatic function, or choose a template/representative. Those features can be imposed by the chemistry of NAD(P) binding and catalysis. Homology or functional transfer should require independent evidence such as consistent SCOPe family/superfamily assignment, sequence similarity, conserved domain architecture/topology, residue-by-residue structural alignment outside the ligand pocket, and phylogenetic or annotation support.
